Name: David Seidman
Question: Would you switch jobs with Bill Gates?
Answer: No. I am eminently unqualified to lead the Gates Foundation. I have no experience managing an organization of that size, no experience in the nonprofit world, and no celebrity to influence the public and world leaders. Also, I don't think he gets paid, which is not going to work for me. Bill Gates is actually reasonably qualified to do my job. He has led organizations the size of mine. Microsoft has a product that directly competes with Salesforce. And Gates has significant experience with computer security. I think he might be overqualified, though.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How do you feel about having a younger manager that has half of your experience?
Answer: I've been the manager in this situation many times. Often it happens because the employee has changed roles over time, like moving from support to general IT to security. Sometimes the employee has just had a slow or unambitious career. And very often the employee simply has no interest in management. I've never had an employee say anything negative about it. It's important to remember that being a manager is a different role. Your job isn't to be an expert, it's to create a team full of experts and help them succeed. A manager can have less engineering experience but still be a great manager. If you as a manager convey this to your team, you'll defuse many potential problems. Where things tend to go badly is when the less experienced manager thinks of their position as superior and thinks, “I give orders, I don't take them.” In my experience, this isn't correlated with years of technical experience. Young managers sometimes think of themselves as hotshot geniuses. Older managers sometimes think of themselves as superior because they've seen it all. However, there is a strong correlation between years of management experience and skill as a manager.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why isn't it common practice for employers to give 2 weeks notice when terminating employees?
Answer: Except in egregious cases of misconduct, companies generally give months of warning that a person's performance is subpar and may lead to termination. This usually culminates in a formal, written Performance Improvement Plan. A PIP states explicitly what an employee needs to do to avoid termination, that termination may result if those things aren't done, and how long the employee has to do those things, with an explicit date that is usually 30–60 days in the future. At the companies I've worked at, the employee is asked to sign the PIP. So they not only get several weeks of notice, they sign a document stating that they are aware of the exact date on which they will be fired. Companies also often offer a poor performer the option to quit voluntarily in exchange for a specific amount of guaranteed severance. A voluntary resignation agreement avoids a drawn out firing process that's unpleasant for everyone, it helps the company reduce the risk of lawsuits and physical violence, and it gives the person being fired a bunch of money that can hopefully get them through the ensuing period of unemployment.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why aren't software engineers afraid that without a union, their salaries will decline and their jobs will go overseas?
Answer: Software has been an important field for over 30 years. During that time, salaries have risen more or less continuously, with occasional bubbles during which substantial numbers of people get very rich. Unemployment in the field is very low, even though companies do send a ton of work overseas. So working in this field means you'll make good money with good job security and have a shot at unbelievable money. So there is very little incentive to form a union.
